t.1.24.1: Then, having heard the excellent words of that immeasurable sage, the tiger among men replied with auspicious speech.
t.1.24.2: O best of sages, since the Yakṣas are said to be of little might, how can a woman, one of the weaker sex, bear the strength of a thousand elephants?
t.1.24.3: Viśvāmitra spoke these words: "Hear by what means she, though a woman and weak by nature, is surpassing in strength and bears a might and power produced by the granting of a boon."
t.1.24.4: Long ago there lived a great Yakṣa named Suketu, mighty and of virtuous conduct, but he was childless, and so he performed great austerities.
t.1.24.5: Then the Grandsire, greatly pleased, gave to that lord of the Yakṣas a jewel of a maiden, O Rāma, who was known by the name of Tāṭakā.
t.1.24.6: The Grandsire gave her the strength of a thousand elephants, but the greatly renowned Brahmā did not give a son to the Yakṣa.
t.1.24.7: When she was born and grew up, endowed with beauty and youth, he gave that illustrious maiden as wife to Sunda, the son of Jambha.
t.1.24.8: Then, after some time, the Yakṣī gave birth to a son, the invincible one named Mārīca, who through a curse became a Rākṣasa.
t.1.24.9: When Sunda was slain, O Rāma, Tāṭakā together with her son sought to assail Agastya, the best of sages.
t.1.24.10: "Take on the state of a Rākṣasa!" So he declared to Mārīca; and Agastya, supremely enraged, cursed Tāṭakā as well.
t.1.24.12: This very Tāṭakā, enraged by the curse laid upon her and swooning with fury, lays waste to this auspicious land once frequented by Agastya.
t.1.24.11: Cast off this form and become a man-eater, a monstrous Yakṣī, misshapen and with a distorted face; let a dreadful form be yours.
t.1.24.13: O Rāghava, for the welfare of cows and brāhmaṇas, slay this wicked and most dreadful yakṣī, whose might is used for evil.
t.1.24.14: For no man in the three worlds is able to slay her, bound as she is by the curse, except you, O Raghunandana.
t.1.24.15: Indeed, you should feel no revulsion at the slaying of a woman, O best of men; for the welfare of the four varṇas, this must be done by a king's son.
t.1.24.16: For those entrusted with the burden of kingship, this is the eternal dharma. Slay this unrighteous woman, O Kākutstha, for there is no dharma in her.
t.1.24.17: For it is heard, O king, that long ago Śakra slew Mantharā, the daughter of Virocana, who wished to destroy the earth.
t.1.24.18: And long ago, O Rāma, the wife of Bhṛgu, firm in her vows and the mother of Kāvya, who desired a world without Indra, was slain by Viṣṇu.
t.1.24.19: By these and by many other great-souled princes, the best of men, women devoted to unrighteousness have been slain.
